rationale: B wins because it keeps the same strong raw material but makes the risk sharper, the beats cleaner, and the proof gates harder to dodge. Its line, "Patients priced out of branded weight-loss drugs now have a cheaper option — with an FDA warning attached," is the honest consumer story; A's "Priced out of branded weight-loss drugs, patients turn to compounded prescriptions instead" sands off the safety conflict and starts sounding like a company brochure. A is good, but B is less impressed with the announcement and more useful to a founder who is about to face real reporters.
gaps_in_A: "A newly profitable Hims & Hers doubles down" uses a blacklisted lazy phrase and makes the regulatory angle sound like startup theater instead of a serious FDA-risk story.
"Freshly profitable Hims & Hers bets its next act" overlaps heavily with "A newly profitable Hims & Hers doubles down"; the investor lens is real, but A makes two angles share too much skeleton.

"Priced out of branded weight-loss drugs, patients turn to compounded prescriptions instead" misses the FDA-risk half of the patient story, which is exactly what keeps it from becoming an access puff piece.
"No good next step yet" is too frozen. The set has viable shapes; the smarter move is to pick the best one and close its gating proof, especially supply source and price.
gaps_in_B: "branded drugmakers want it stopped" is stronger than the fact block, which only says manufacturers have pushed back. Useful framing, but it needs proof before it becomes copy.
"Hims & Hers is scaling them anyway" slightly overstates the launch fact; access is launching, scale is not established in the provided update.

"affordability squeeze on branded GLP-1s is the context readers already live in" imports broader market context. It is plausible, but the fact packet only gives price contrast, not patient affordability data.

The next step says "pick one and resolve real names" but should explicitly name which proof gate comes first for each route: supplier for regulatory/conflict, dollars for affordability, required-vs-optional testing for diagnostics.
